summary: Discovery focused on reserved GPU topology, tenant hardening during surge windows, and fallback to hosted instances. Customer shared traffic patterns (daily batch + unpredictable spikes), strict encryption/KMS needs, and a preference for deterministic SLA for peak inference. Redwood AE + SE proposed a reserved warm-pool + prewarm windows model with automatic fallback to hosted for extreme spikes. Agreed next steps: share security docs, run pilot benchmark, and propose SOW.
transcript:
Header: 2027-04-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: 57m | Attendees: Samir, Lina, Owen (Redwood); Maya, Derek, Priya, Tom (Neoterra)

Topics: reserved capacity, tenant fencing, warm pools/prewarm, burst windows, KMS/HSM, SOC2, fallback routing, cost tradeoffs

00:00 Speaker 1 (Samir): okay everyone, thanks for joining. we're at 15:00 UTC, quick intros?
00:08 Speaker 2 (Maya): hey, I'm Maya, head of ML at Neoterra, we own model infra and product integration.
00:14 Speaker 3 (Derek): Derek, platform eng, I manage our k8s clusters and infra orchestration.
00:18 Speaker 4 (Priya): Priya, security. I'll own compliance checks and encryption requirements.
00:22 Speaker 1 (Samir): great, from Redwood we've got Lina on the systems side and Owen who's focused on deployment topology.
00:28 Speaker 5 (Tom): Tom here, CTO, sorry I'm late, joining now.
00:32 Speaker 1 (Samir): no worries. quick goal for this call—understand your production burst patterns and isolation needs so we can size a reserved pool and propose a fallback strategy.
00:44 Speaker 3 (Derek): high level—our workload is mostly steady daytime traffic with three scheduled batch jobs at 02:00 local, plus occasional unpredictable spikes when clients run heavy analytic queries. spikes can be 3–5x baseline for 5–20 minutes.
01:02 Speaker 2 (Maya): also model sizes vary—some endpoints are small encoder models, others are large 30B-ish transformers used for summary on demand. we care about 95th and 99th token-latency.
01:18 Speaker 4 (Priya): compliance: we need encryption at rest with customer-managed KMS/HSM, SOC2 type II, SSO (SAML) integration, and audit logs for every inference request for 90 days. any egress/residency constraints are minimal—mainly we need a private VPC option for production.
01:40 Speaker 1 (Samir): good to know. Redwood Dedicated supports private deployments with KMS integration and audit logs; we can run the control plane in a VPC and the inference nodes in your cloud account or ours depending on the Private vs Dedicated trade.
01:56 Speaker 3 (Derek): question—we'd prefer predictable throughput at peak so we don't block customers. Can reserved capacity guarantee throughput for the hot endpoints? how do you handle tenant fencing—i.e., preventing noisy neighbor interference?
02:12 Speaker 6 (Lina): short answer: reserved pools give guaranteed slot counts and pre-provisioned GPUs, and we provide tenant fencing via either strict node pinning or logical isolation at the serving layer. for hot endpoints we recommend warm-pools: keep a scaled set of models preloaded for expected peaks, plus an ephemeral burst policy.
02:34 Speaker 2 (Maya): ephemeral burst policy... how does that interact with cost—if we provision big warm pools we're paying even when idle.
02:44 Speaker 6 (Lina): yep tradeoff; warm pools reduce cold-start latency but increase baseline cost. our optimize toolkit can recommend prewarm sizing based on your p95/p99 latency SLOs; alternatively you can use smaller reserved core + fallback to stored-hosted capacity during infrequent big spikes.
03:02 Speaker 5 (Tom): fallback to hosted—so you'd route overflow to Redwood hosted models? how do we handle data residency and encryption in that flow?
03:12 Speaker 1 (Samir): we can define routing policies: primary route to your dedicated pool; if queue depth exceeds threshold or latency rises above threshold, requests overflow to a hosted, equivalent model variant. For data sensitivity, we can encrypt payloads in transit and provide contract terms about data usage; for the pilot we can pseudonymize payloads or route only non-sensitive traffic to hosted.
03:38 Speaker 4 (Priya): we need to validate that hosted fallback doesn't retain raw customer data. is there an auto-evict or no-retention setting?
03:46 Speaker 6 (Lina): hosted endpoints can be configured with zero retention and strict access controls; we'll also provide an architecture note and runbook describing data handling.
03:56 Speaker 2 (Maya): back to capacity—what's the failure mode during a storm if the reserved pool is fully saturated and hosted fallback is delayed? we'd prefer graceful degradation, not hard errors to clients.
04:08 Speaker 7 (Owen): we implement circuit-breaker style responses—if both reserved and hosted are at capacity we can enforce queued backpressure with best-effort priority routing (e.g., route billing-critical traffic first), or return a 429 with a structured retry-after header and optional cached response. we also can integrate a local KV/prefix cache for common prefixes to reduce token compute.
04:38 Speaker 3 (Derek): interesting—what about prewarming schedule and quiet windows? our heavy spikes often occur in a narrow 10–30 minute window, and we want to prewarm for that without keeping capacity idle for hours.
04:54 Speaker 6 (Lina): you can schedule prewarm jobs—warm the pool 15–20 minutes before the expected window and then scale down. we also support ad-hoc prewarm via API if your scheduling misses. the cost model supports short prewarm commit with lower hourly credit than full reserved capacity—it's a hybrid.
05:12 Speaker 2 (Maya): can we do a rapid failover to a lower-capacity quantized model variant to reduce cost in emergency? like swap 30B float -> 8-bit quantized 13B during spikes?
05:24 Speaker 6 (Lina): yes, model variants are part of the platform; we can pin promos and automatic roll-forward/roll-back policies. during fallback you can select cheaper quantized variants; there's a possible quality delta and we'll surface regressed evals.
05:40 Speaker 5 (Tom): curious if you support multi-tenant hotpool sharding—so we isolate tenant compute on separate GPUs during surge windows to reduce blast radius.
05:50 Speaker 7 (Owen): we do. logical tenant sharding can be done via label-based scheduling or by dedicated node groups per tenant. dedicated nodes per tenant is stronger isolation but increases cost; label-based scheduling is more flexible.
06:06 Speaker 4 (Priya): for audit, we need per-token-level traceability and per-request provenance. can you provide token-level cost accounting per customer?
06:18 Speaker 6 (Lina): yes, we provide token-level billing and tracing; Console exports show per-route/token breakdowns and traces. we can also push logs to your SIEM with structured JSON.
06:28 Speaker 3 (Derek): what about networking—I want the inference nodes in our VPC, can the control plane still live in Redwood's cloud?
06:36 Speaker 1 (Samir): absolutely; that's our Private deployment pattern: control plane optionally in our managed zone with data plane in your VPC, or full Private where control plane runs in your account. either way we support secure peering and private endpoints.
06:50 Speaker 2 (Maya): latency question—our SLA target is 95th token latency under 200ms for the biggest models. is that realistic?
07:00 Speaker 6 (Lina): depends on sequence length and model; for 30B models with good batching and prewarm we can hit p95 ~150–220ms on A100-class GPUs for single-stream inference; sequence length and KV cache hit rates matter. we'll validate in a pilot.
07:18 Speaker 5 (Tom): pilot—what would that look like? we want to run our 3 production endpoints for two weeks, measure p95/p99 and cost.
07:26 Speaker 1 (Samir): typical pilot: 2-week reserved pool with a small commitment (we can size conservatively), Redwood runs benchmark harness + traces, compare against your in-house baseline. Lina would own the benchmark config.
07:40 Speaker 4 (Priya): security acceptance criteria for pilot—SOC2 doc, network diagram, encryption flow, and an NDA addendum for pilot data handling.
07:50 Speaker 6 (Lina): we'll include those in the security packet.
07:54 Speaker 3 (Derek): on autoscaling policies—how quick can we scale GPUs up? cold provisioning GPUs takes minutes in some cloud regions.
08:04 Speaker 7 (Owen): true; that's why we recommend warm-pools or prewarmed standby nodes. fast scale beyond reserved capacity often relies on burst to hosted or prewarmed ephemeral instances that are already booted. cold GPU attach from cloud may take 3–8 minutes.
08:22 Speaker 2 (Maya): ok makes sense. can Redwood integrate with our internal traffic router for route decisions? we'd prefer to manage routing rules from our side.
08:30 Speaker 1 (Samir): yes, we expose routing APIs and can integrate with your sidecar or LB. many customers keep control of high-level routing while Redwood handles the inference plumbing.
08:40 Speaker 4 (Priya): compliance—what's your KMS integration patterns? CMK? HSM?
08:46 Speaker 6 (Lina): we support both customer-managed KMS (CMK) and HSM-backed keys for high-assurance workloads; for Private deployments we can integrate to your KMS via VPC endpoints.
08:58 Speaker 5 (Tom): pricing transparency—how do you bill reserved pool hours vs prewarm vs hosted overflow?
09:06 Speaker 1 (Samir): reserved pools billed per-hour for the committed GPUs, prewarm has reduced hourly pricing, and overflow to hosted charged per-token + a small routing fee. we'll send the tiered pricing sheet.
09:16 Speaker 3 (Derek): two more technicals: checkpointing model state between prewarm sessions, and KV cache persistence—if we tear down a prewarm node, can cached kvs be persisted to warm start?
09:28 Speaker 7 (Owen): we persist KV caches to a fast backing store for warm start in some configurations; full cross-node KV sharing has limitations for multi-GPU distributed models, but for single-node serving we can snapshot and restore. we'll document the tradeoffs.
09:48 Speaker 2 (Maya): what about logging—we need redaction for PII before logs leave our VPC.
09:54 Speaker 6 (Lina): we support in-VPC log redaction hooks and can forward sanitized logs to your SIEM; redaction rules can run in your account.
10:04 Speaker 5 (Tom): great. any questions from your side?
10:08 Speaker 1 (Samir): yeah, quick ask of Neoterra—can you share a few days of traffic histograms and identify 2–3 representative endpoints for the pilot?
10:16 Speaker 2 (Maya): yes we'll share that; Derek will pull histograms and sequence length distributions.
10:22 Speaker 4 (Priya): and we'll confirm compliance checklist items and whether we need an on-prem path.
10:28 Speaker 1 (Samir): awesome. to recap—Redwood will: send security pack + pricing, Lina will run a cost/latency projection, schedule pilot benchmark with Derek next week, and draft SOW. Customer will share traffic histograms and confirm encryption needs.
10:44 Speaker 2 (Maya): sounds good. thanks.
10:46 Speaker 5 (Tom): thank you, appreciate the clarity.
10:50 Speaker 1 (Samir): thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the attachments. meeting closed.

Notes about transcription: occasional speaker mislabels (Speaker 6 is Lina, Speaker 7 is Owen). Some acronyms transcribed oddly (HSM sometimes 'H-S-M', KV cache occasionally 'K V'). There were short crosstalks and filler words omitted.
